descriptionChirho: Adjective describing personal might or power, applied to God or strong individuals. Arabic عَظيمٌ/عُظَماءَ 'great/mighty ones' and عاتِيَةٌ 'fierce/violent' reflect personal power. Spanish 'poderoso' (powerful) and 'poderosos' (powerful ones) are consistent. Korean 능력하신 'the capable/mighty one' and 강한 자들을 'the strong ones' emphasize personal strength. Hindi शक्तिशाली 'powerful' and शक्तिशालियों 'powerful ones' and प्रचण्ड 'fierce/intense' all point to personal might. Swahili mkuu/wenye nguvu 'great/having strength' confirms. Singular and plural inflections of the same adjectival sense are merged.

Adjective describing greatness of impersonal things like waters, forces, or general magnitude. Arabic كَثِيرَةٍ 'many/abundant' and جَارِفَةٍ 'sweeping/torrential' describe powerful natural forces. Spanish 'impetuosas' (impetuous, of waters) and 'mayor' (greater) point to non-personal magnitude. Korean 큰 'great/large' is used for impersonal scale. Hindi बहुत 'much/very' and बड़ा 'great/large' describe quantity or size rather than personal power. Swahili mengi 'many' and makubwa 'large' confirm impersonal magnitude. This includes comparative usage (S105377 'greater') which describes relative magnitude.

Adjective emphasizing sheer quantity or abundance rather than power or size. Arabic عَظيماً here functions as 'greatly/abundantly' rather than 'mighty.' Spanish 'abundante' (abundant) is the clearest differentiator from the power sense. Korean 많은 것을 'many things' and Hindi बहुत 'much/a lot' focus on amount. Swahili mengi 'many/much' confirms quantitative meaning. This sense is distinguished from the 'mighty' senses because the context emphasizes quantity of substance or material rather than strength or greatness of persons or forces.
